sections.heading: Operational principle
sections.text: Someone runs the command at a terminal, picks Make a model, names a folder and the company; the instance is made with core vendored under its unit's folder, every vendored file in the manifest with its hash and the workflow pinned to the same release, so the check passes at once; when a later release is run, Move a model lists what it would write and remove, and moves core, skills, manifest and workflow ref together on a yes.

sections.heading: Scenarios
sections.text:
### SC-M1: A new folder becomes an instance that passes

Given a folder that does not exist, when Make a model is picked and the company named, then the instance is made with its manifest and starting entities, and checking the folder passes.

### SC-M2: A folder already claimed is refused whole

Given a folder that holds a `meta/` folder of its own, when the model is added beside its files, then nothing is written and the refusal names `meta/` as already there.

### SC-M3: A move is shown before it is made

Given an instance on an older release, when Move a model is picked, then every path the move would write or remove is listed, and the instance is moved to the release only on a yes to Go ahead.

### SC-M4: An edited vendored file stops the move

Given a vendored file edited inside the instance, when the instance is moved, then nothing is written and the file is named; moved with `--force`, it is overwritten and named as overwritten.

### SC-M5: A pack taken later

Given an instance made without a pack, when it is moved with `--pack software`, then the pack is vendored as a unit beside core, listed in the manifest and each root folder it adds is given a README once.

entities.name: A chat answer marks the claims its evidence does not carry
entities.tagline: Someone reading an answer from a company's model sees which of its sentences the entities it names do not bear out, before deciding which of them to trust.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: Each claim of an answer, a sentence, a list item or a table row, is read back against the text of the tool answers that carried the entities it names, exactly as the model was given it, by a decision model outside the machine that picks a verdict with a probability and writes nothing. Where a deployment checks its answers, the chat marks a claim the evidence carries only in part, or not at all, once the answer is drawn, with a note saying which, and a line under the answer says how many it marked. It marks only above a probability measured on real answers, marks nothing in an answer written in German until German is measured on its own, and marks nothing where the check could not run. It stops at the mark: it changes no answer, it says whether a claim keeps to what the model says and never whether the model is right, and every checked answer is counted in the week's report whether it was marked or not.

entities.name: A company of more than one person describes its units and who answers to whom
entities.tagline: A company of more than one person writes down its units and the teams drawn from them, the jobs its people are employed in, who answers to whom and who sets the discipline of whose work, and which positions it is looking to fill.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
The organization pack, taken beside core: a group is a unit of the company or a team drawn from its units, of a kind the company names, and a job is what a person is employed as wherever they sit. A person sits in a unit in a job, and the disciplinary line runs from each person to their unit's lead and up through the units; the professional line runs from a group to the jobs it guides, wherever the people in them sit. A group names the positions it is looking to fill, a staff unit stands beside the head it serves, and a rank on each group is the company's own order.

It stops at the structure. It draws no org chart, which is a renderer's to draw from the pages, and holds no headcount and no cost.

entities.name: A company that builds software describes how it designs it
entities.tagline: A company that builds software writes down its bounded contexts, the terms each one's language holds, the aggregates and events inside them and how a feature is built across them, in the words of domain-driven design, as a refinement of the concepts and features it already describes.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
The software pack, taken beside core: a bounded context with how much it matters to build well, the terms of its language as entities and value objects, the aggregates that keep them consistent with the commands they handle, the domain events other contexts consume, and a feature design saying how one feature is built across the contexts it touches. A term refines a core concept and a feature design a core feature, so a reader goes from what the company means by a word to how its software keeps it.

It stops at the design. It generates no code and reads none, so nothing holds the code to the pages. An architecture decision is a core decision the pack's pages name, not a type of its own.

entities.name: A company that runs systems describes its landscape
entities.tagline: A company that runs systems writes down which ones it has, what each runs on, what each offers the others, which one keeps the data of each thing it knows about and where each takes its data from, so whoever plans a replacement or answers for an outage reads it in one place.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
The landscape pack, taken beside core: a system is of a kind the company names in its own words, and each kind is a specialization of one ArchiMate element, so a generator can take a system to an architecture tool and back as the element it is. A system says what it runs on, who owns it and who runs it, the features it realizes and the data processor behind it; a service is what a system exposes to others, with the systems that provide it. A system names the concepts it keeps data of, one of them the master of each, with the data object it keeps of a concept where one is modeled, and a connection is written on the system that takes the data, with the interface it goes through.

It stops at the inventory. It ships the mapping to the standard and no generator, draws no diagram, which a consumer draws from the pages, holds no cost and no license, and says nothing about where a system is.

entities.name: A decision model asks each page its schema's writing rules
entities.tagline: A company learns which of its pages most likely break a writing rule before anyone reads them, and decides first exactly what leaves its hands to find out.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: Each bullet of a schema's writing rules becomes a typed question, asked of every page of that type, and a decision model outside the machine answers each with a choice and how likely it is. Before anything is sent, the owner is shown the pages, the questions, the service, what the run will cost and a digest of it all, and only a yes to that digest sends exactly those files; a no sends nothing. The report flags the pages whose answers fall below a band measured against the one model it names, and the agent pass reads those first. It stops at advice: it changes no page, a flag counts only once it has been read against its page, and the agent pass still reads every page the report does not flag. Which model answers is the tooling's pinned choice, and another is measured before it is named.

entities.name: A profile is written from a person's documents
entities.tagline: Someone hands an agent a folder of a person's CVs, diplomas, certificates and reference letters and gets back a profile the model can hold: the periods, the skills they show and the levels those skills earned.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: A procedure an agent follows, shipped as a skill with every instance and moved with it on every upgrade, because what a period shows and what level a claim has earned are judgments no script makes. It asks whether to create a profile or extend one, reads every document in the folder, reuses the skills, levels, kinds and seats the model already holds and proposes only what is missing, writes the experiences and the profile against their schemas, and runs the checks and the agent pass. The operator decides every level, every seat and every sentence said in the person's own voice, and the commit is theirs. A CV is derived from what it writes: the profile says what the person claims and the experiences it owns say what happened, when and where, each claim resting on its evidence, so the CV is drawn from them and never kept beside them. Deriving one is not part of this feature. It stops at the documents: a fact no schema has a place for is left out and written down nowhere, and publishing the profile is a separate step.

entities.name: A repository is held to one form and told which pins are behind
entities.tagline: Every repository around a company's model, its site, its services and its server, follows one Markdown form and learns which of the releases and commits it takes have moved on, without anything moving them for it.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: `form` holds every Markdown file to one fixed form; a repository may only exclude paths, and `check` and the instance workflow run it. An instance declares in `pins.json` what it takes from another repository, a release or a commit, and `pins` asks each upstream and says current, behind, unknown, unmanaged or missing. It moves nothing, because a pin that is behind is intent until someone calls it drift. A repository with no model takes the same with `adopt`: a manifest without core, the workflow, the seat hook and its own `pins.json`. The machinery is the meta-model's; the rules a company writes stay its own.

entities.name: A visitor asks the model
entities.tagline: Someone on a page asks a company's model a question in their own words and gets an answer that names the entity each claim rests on.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: A chat over any instance's MCP server, opened from a button on a site's page: it asks the server's tools what the model says, writes the answer from what they returned, and names and links the entity each claim rests on, so a visitor can check it without connecting an agent of their own. It holds no model and pins no commit; it answers from whatever the server it is deployed beside serves. It stops at the question: what the model says is the server's, where it runs and what it may spend is each deployment's own, and where the model does not say, the answer says so rather than filling the gap.

entities.name: A vocabulary to describe a company in
entities.tagline: A company can write down what it knows as entities of named types, each held to a schema, instead of in whatever shape the last tool left it in.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: The core types, one schema per type, the conventions that make a graph of Markdown files checkable, and a worked example, vendored into an instance at a release the instance names. It stops at the vocabulary: which types a company fills, and what it writes in them, is the company's.

entities.name: An agent does the work no script can, by the skills an instance ships
entities.tagline: Someone asks an agent to build a company's model from its web address, write a person's profile from their documents, check every page against its schema's writing rules or publish the model somewhere, and the agent follows the procedure that ships with the instance instead of improvising one.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: The procedures an agent follows where the work is a judgment and not a rule: building an instance from what a company publishes, writing or extending a profile from a person's documents, recording the terms a source is published under and the consent it needs, validating an instance with the agent pass beside the mechanical checks, producing the content of a surface, and exporting the instance for an agent or a notebook to read. `init` installs them, each where the agent the instance was made for reads it, and every upgrade moves them with core, so an instance follows the procedures of the release it names. Each skill proposes, writes against the schemas and runs the checks; the operator decides every level, seat and sentence, and the commit is theirs. It stops at the files: merging stays with a person, and a procedure a company writes for itself is its own and not part of this feature.

entities.name: An agent reads the model
entities.tagline: An agent asks a company's model which types it declares, what one entity says and what evidence a claim rests on, and gets the answer the model gives at one commit.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: A server speaking the Model Context Protocol over any instance, parsed from one pinned commit: it lists the types a company declares, returns an entity with its references resolved, searches the model and finds the evidence a claim rests on. It only reads. It writes nothing back, adds nothing of its own, and answers at the commit its deployment names, so two agents asking one question get one answer. It stops at the server: where it runs, and over which instance, is each deployment's own.

entities.name: An instance is made and kept from one command
entities.tagline: Someone starts a company's model, checks it, moves it to a newer vocabulary and puts the editor beside it, from one menu and without installing anything first.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: The CLI is one command, `npx --yes 'github:companygraph/meta-model#semver:*'`, run from the newest release on GitHub; it opens a menu that does all of it: it makes an instance in a folder, with the vocabulary vendored, a manifest naming every file it owns, a folder per type, the entities no instance passes without, a workflow and the agent files, so that the instance passes the checks on its first day; it runs the mechanical checks as the instance's own workflow runs them; it moves an instance to a newer release, its vendored core, its skills, its manifest and its workflow together; and it installs the Obsidian plugin in a vault or updates it there. Each pick reports what it did and the menu comes back. It stops at the instance's shape and its tooling: what a company writes into the folders is the company's, and writing a page from its schema is not among the picks.

entities.name: Checks an instance runs
entities.tagline: A company finds out before a change lands whether its pages still hold to the schemas it adopted.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: The mechanical half of validation: a checker shipped in every release, which an instance's workflow calls at the release its manifest names. It reads the schemas from the core the instance vendored, never from its own, so taking a newer release never holds an instance to rules it has not adopted, and a checker that is not the named release refuses to run. It stops at what a script can read: whether a page keeps its schema's writing rules is the agent pass, and every run says so.

entities.name: Checks while a file is edited
entities.tagline: Someone writing a page sees what its schema requires, and what they broke, while they type rather than when the change is pushed.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: A plugin for Obsidian over any instance. It runs the checks a release ships as a file is edited and marks what fails where it is written, completes a reference or a section from what the schemas declare, and renames an entity everywhere its name is used. It bundles the checker of the release it was built with and refuses a vendored core newer than that, rather than check a vault against rules it does not know. It stops at the editor: the gate a change has to pass is still the checks an instance runs.

entities.name: The vocabulary on the web
entities.tagline: Anyone can read the vocabulary, and see it describe a company, in a browser and without cloning a repository.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: The model page is the model, drawn: every type of core and of each pack the vocabulary ships, with its schema, as the graph of what references what, from a pinned commit of the vocabulary. The page around the drawing reads in English and Swiss Standard German; the drawing itself stays in the vocabulary's one language, English. The example page is one company, drawn: a fictional company described in that vocabulary, from the same commit. Both are also published as files an agent can fetch. It stops at reading: nothing on the web writes to a model, and what the site must say and how it is built belong to the companygraph.io website.

entities.name: Team
entities.tagline: A group that gathers people and agents for the work on CompanyGraph, and stands outside the disciplinary line.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text: A team is for the work on CompanyGraph. It stands outside the disciplinary line because nothing CompanyGraph publishes says it hires anyone, appraises anyone or sets anyone's objectives. A unit that did those things would stand in the line, and would not be a team.

entities.name: Maintainers
entities.tagline: Keeps CompanyGraph, from deciding what it is for through every gate to the merge, the tag and the release.

entities.name: Entity id
entities.tagline: An entity keeps this id through every rename and every language it is written in, so whatever holds one outside the model still finds the entity.

entities.name: CompanyGraph
entities.tagline: The open-source meta-model for operating a company: the structure a company's knowledge takes, so that the people who run it and the agents working beside them can both rely on it.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text:
We publish a vocabulary for describing a company as a graph of Markdown files — one file per entity, folders named for their type, and a schema saying what each type carries. It is written for the people who run a company and for the agents that increasingly work beside them, because both need the same answer to the same question and only one of them can ask a colleague.

What the model holds is a projection of what a company already knows. Every page names the source with authority over its facts — this repository, where a fact is written and corrected in place, or a system the company already runs, which a sync writes from and where a correction belongs instead. Describing a company this way moves nothing out of the systems it runs on, and what anyone writes here stays theirs.

entities.name: Co-Maintainer
entities.tagline: Has a say in what CompanyGraph is for and at every gate before Integrate, and leaves the merge, the tag and the release to the Maintainer.

entities.name: Maintainer
entities.tagline: Decides what CompanyGraph is for, and gives the word every merge, tag and release waits on.

entities.name: Carried Claim Rate
entities.tagline: The share of a week's claims, in the answers a chat checked, that the evidence the answer was written from carries.

serves: An agent answers as well as the person who runs the company
fields.unit: percent of checked claims per week

sections.heading: How it is measured
sections.text:
The chats this KPI counts are the surfaces of this model that answer a visitor's question from it and check their answers. A claim is a sentence, a list item or a table row of an answer. Where a deployment checks, each claim is judged against the text of the tool answers that carried the entities it names, exactly as the model was given it, and the kept line of the message counts its `claims` and its `unsupported`: those judged `partial`, `contradicted`, `absent`, `withheld`, `unnamed` or `unsourced`. A message whose check could not run, or that was refused, carries neither count and is left out.

Each chat's weekly report sums both counts over the answers it checked in the ISO week that ended, Monday midnight UTC to the next, under its Claims section; the value, read per chat, is the week's claims less those not carried, divided by its claims. Every verdict counts whatever its probability, so the value does not move with the threshold above which the chat marks a claim, and a German answer counts though the chat marks none.

sections.heading: What it can hide
sections.text: A claim is judged against what the tools returned, so a claim that repeats a page which is itself wrong counts as carried: the rate says the answers kept to the model, not that the model is true. It rises when answers say less, since an answer with fewer claims has fewer to miss, and a chat that stops using the tools makes no claims the check can count; Grounded Answer Rate, read beside it, shows answers that no longer rest on the model. A claim judged `partial` counts as not carried however much of it was. And the judge is another company's model at a release of its own, so a new release can move the rate with no answer changed; a week that moves without a change to the chat or the model is read against the judge's release first.

entities.name: Change Fail Rate
entities.tagline: The share of deployments that need immediate intervention once they are in production.

sections.heading: How it is measured
sections.text:
A deployment is a merge to `main` in a repository whose workflows publish one of this model's surfaces — the companygraph.io website, which GitHub Pages publishes, and the mcp.companygraph.io MCP server and the chat.companygraph.io chat, which that repository's deploy and chat workflows publish — and a release of meta-model, mcp-server, chat-server or the Obsidian plugin, because a release is what someone adopting CompanyGraph installs. A merge counts once, however many of its workflows publish. The MCP Registry listing, republished when the MCP server's repository tags a release, is not a deployment.

The deployments of a calendar month in UTC that were followed, before the next planned change to the same surface or package, by a revert, a fix or a re-pin made because of them, divided by all deployments of that month. Deployments and their times are read from the merges to `main` in the GitHub history of companygraph/companygraph.github.io and companygraph/mcp-companygraph-io; their publishing runs are GitHub Pages' own `pages-build-deployment` runs for the site and mcp-companygraph-io's `deploy` and `chat` workflow runs on `main`; a release is read from the GitHub releases of companygraph/meta-model, companygraph/mcp-server, companygraph/chat-server and companygraph/obsidian-plugin. A failure is what a visitor, an agent or a check against the live surface met, or what an instance that installed the release met, not a workflow run that failed before publishing anything.

sections.heading: What it can hide
sections.text: It falls when fewer changes ship, and when a failure is folded into the next planned change instead of being named as one. Deployment Frequency, read beside it, shows the first; the second shows only if failures are named when they happen.

entities.name: Change Lead Time
entities.tagline: The time a change takes from being committed to version control to running in production.

sections.heading: How it is measured
sections.text:
A deployment is a merge to `main` in a repository whose workflows publish one of this model's surfaces — the companygraph.io website, which GitHub Pages publishes, and the mcp.companygraph.io MCP server and the chat.companygraph.io chat, which that repository's deploy and chat workflows publish — and a release of meta-model, mcp-server, chat-server or the Obsidian plugin, because a release is what someone adopting CompanyGraph installs. A merge counts once, however many of its workflows publish. The MCP Registry listing, republished when the MCP server's repository tags a release, is not a deployment.

For each deployment, the time from the earliest commit it carries that no earlier deployment carried to the moment it is live, or for a release, published; a change to the model counts from its commit in companygraph/mental-model to the deployment of the re-pin that carries it. The value is the median over the deployments of a calendar month in UTC, read from the merges to `main` and their times in the GitHub history of companygraph/companygraph.github.io and companygraph/mcp-companygraph-io, from `pages-build-deployment` runs for the site and mcp-companygraph-io's `deploy` and `chat` runs on `main`, and, for a release, from the commit history and GitHub releases of companygraph/meta-model, companygraph/mcp-server, companygraph/chat-server and companygraph/obsidian-plugin.

sections.heading: What it can hide
sections.text: It shortens when changes get smaller and when review gets thinner, and only the first is progress. Thinner review shows as a higher Change Fail Rate, which is why the two are read together. A median also hides the change that waited a week behind a re-pin.

entities.name: Deployment Frequency
entities.tagline: How often a change reaches production.

sections.heading: How it is measured
sections.text:
A deployment is a merge to `main` in a repository whose workflows publish one of this model's surfaces — the companygraph.io website, which GitHub Pages publishes, and the mcp.companygraph.io MCP server and the chat.companygraph.io chat, which that repository's deploy and chat workflows publish — and a release of meta-model, mcp-server, chat-server or the Obsidian plugin, because a release is what someone adopting CompanyGraph installs. A merge counts once, however many of its workflows publish. The MCP Registry listing, republished when the MCP server's repository tags a release, is not a deployment.

The number of deployments in an ISO week, Monday midnight UTC to the next. Deployments and their times are read from the merges to `main` in the GitHub history of companygraph/companygraph.github.io and companygraph/mcp-companygraph-io; their publishing runs are GitHub Pages' own `pages-build-deployment` runs for the site and mcp-companygraph-io's `deploy` and `chat` workflow runs on `main`; a release is read from the GitHub releases of companygraph/meta-model, companygraph/mcp-server, companygraph/chat-server and companygraph/obsidian-plugin. A workflow run that failed and published nothing is not a deployment.

sections.heading: What it can hide
sections.text: It rises when one change is split into several deployments and when something ships that did not need to; the first is the point and the second is noise. A rise bought with rushed changes shows in Change Fail Rate. A week without deployments reads the same whether nothing was ready or nothing was worth shipping.

entities.name: Deployment Rework Rate
entities.tagline: The share of deployments that were not planned and happened because of an incident in production.

sections.heading: How it is measured
sections.text:
A deployment is a merge to `main` in a repository whose workflows publish one of this model's surfaces — the companygraph.io website, which GitHub Pages publishes, and the mcp.companygraph.io MCP server and the chat.companygraph.io chat, which that repository's deploy and chat workflows publish — and a release of meta-model, mcp-server, chat-server or the Obsidian plugin, because a release is what someone adopting CompanyGraph installs. A merge counts once, however many of its workflows publish. The MCP Registry listing, republished when the MCP server's repository tags a release, is not a deployment.

The deployments of a calendar month in UTC made because something in production was wrong or an installed release was broken, a revert, a hotfix, an emergency re-pin or an unplanned patch release, divided by all deployments of that month. Deployments and their times are read from the merges to `main` in the GitHub history of companygraph/companygraph.github.io and companygraph/mcp-companygraph-io; their publishing runs are GitHub Pages' own `pages-build-deployment` runs for the site and mcp-companygraph-io's `deploy` and `chat` workflow runs on `main`; a release is read from the GitHub releases of companygraph/meta-model, companygraph/mcp-server, companygraph/chat-server and companygraph/obsidian-plugin. Whether a deployment is rework is read from why it was made, which its pull request says, not from its size.

sections.heading: What it can hide
sections.text: It falls when fixes are held back and shipped inside planned work, so the incident lasts longer and the rate looks better. Deployment Frequency, read beside it, shows whether planned deployments are still going out.

entities.name: Failed Deployment Recovery Time
entities.tagline: The time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and needs immediate intervention.

sections.heading: How it is measured
sections.text:
A deployment is a merge to `main` in a repository whose workflows publish one of this model's surfaces — the companygraph.io website, which GitHub Pages publishes, and the mcp.companygraph.io MCP server and the chat.companygraph.io chat, which that repository's deploy and chat workflows publish — and a release of meta-model, mcp-server, chat-server or the Obsidian plugin, because a release is what someone adopting CompanyGraph installs. A merge counts once, however many of its workflows publish. The MCP Registry listing, republished when the MCP server's repository tags a release, is not a deployment.

For each failed deployment, as Change Fail Rate counts them, the time from that deployment going live to the deployment that restores the surface going live, whether a revert, a fix, a re-pin to an earlier release or the release that supersedes a failed one being published. The value is the median over a calendar quarter in UTC. Deployments and their times are read from the merges to `main` in the GitHub history of companygraph/companygraph.github.io and companygraph/mcp-companygraph-io; their publishing runs are GitHub Pages' own `pages-build-deployment` runs for the site and mcp-companygraph-io's `deploy` and `chat` workflow runs on `main`; a release is read from the GitHub releases of companygraph/meta-model, companygraph/mcp-server, companygraph/chat-server and companygraph/obsidian-plugin. A failure no deployment caused, a provider's outage, is not counted.

sections.heading: What it can hide
sections.text: It shortens when every failure is reverted rather than fixed, which restores the surface and leaves the change undone, so the change comes back as rework. Failures are rare here, so a quarter's median can rest on one or two events, and one slow recovery moves it a long way.

entities.name: Grounded Answer Rate
entities.tagline: The share of a week's questions, asked at any chat that answers from the model, whose answer rested on what the model's tools returned.

serves: An agent answers as well as the person who runs the company

sections.heading: How it is measured
sections.text:
The chats this KPI counts are the surfaces of this model that answer a visitor's question from it, whatever MCP hosts stand behind them. Every message one of them accepted from a page it is deployed for leaves one line in that chat's log: the question, its language, the entities the answer cited, how many tool calls the answer made, how many of them found nothing, and whether the fence refused it. The answer itself is not kept. A question counts as answered when the fence did not refuse it and the model had material from the tools: an entity it cited, or more calls than found nothing, since a list answer names rows without citing one entity. A call found nothing when the host refused it, when it failed, or when it returned a list with no rows.

Each chat's weekly report reads its lines of the ISO week that ended, Monday midnight UTC to the next, and applies that rule; the value is read per chat, the questions its report counts as answered divided by all its questions of the week, refused ones included. The rule lives in the report and not in the server that writes the line, so it can change while the lines stand.

sections.heading: What it can hide
sections.text: An answer that cites the right entity and says something wrong about it counts as answered: the rate measures whether the answer rested on the model, not whether what it said was carried by what it rested on. The answer is not kept, but where a chat checks its answers the kept line counts the claims each made and those their evidence does not carry, and Carried Claim Rate, read beside it, shows the difference. It rises when the model reads the identity entity for every question, since one cite is enough, so a week where every answer cites the same entity reads as well as one where each cites the entity the question was about; the report's table of most cited entities shows the difference. It falls when the fence refuses, for a spent share or a host that is down, which is the fence working and not the answer failing; the report's table of unanswered questions separates a refusal from an answer without material. A question that was not about the model, which the Answerer meets with one sentence and no tool, counts as not answered though it got the right reply.

entities.name: Merges Past Their Checks
entities.tagline: The merges that reached a default branch of ours in one week while a required check had not passed.

assesses: Main takes a change only through a green, current pull request
serves: Every gate an agent's work passes is held by a person

sections.heading: How it is measured
sections.text: GitHub records a rule suite with the result `bypass` each time a change reaches a default branch although a rule of its ruleset did not pass, which only an admin can do. Every Monday, the `kpi` workflow of companygraph/mcp-companygraph-io reads the ISO week that ended, Monday 00:00 to Monday 00:00 UTC, across the companygraph organization's repositories with the organization's GitHub App, and classifies each bypass from its pull request. A merge counts here when a required check had not completed with success by the merge — still queued, running or failed — or when the change had no pull request, broke a rule other than the required checks, or could not be read. A merge whose branch was only behind main, with every required check passed, does not count. The week's object, `ruleset-bypasses/<year>-W<week>.json` in the bucket `kpi-reports-companygraph-io-mcp`, holds this count as `past_checks`, beside `behind_main` and the total.

sections.heading: What it can hide
sections.text: A repository with no ruleset is never evaluated, and a check that is not required does not count. A merge behind main is not counted although its checks ran against an older main. A required check that a path filter skipped counts as not passed although nothing was skipped on purpose. Where the App cannot read a ruleset's history, the required checks are counted from the rule suite at the merge, and a check required today but not then can, if it ran green, stand in for one that never started. Change Fail Rate, read beside it, shows whether these merges failed more often than the rest.

entities.name: Languages
entities.tagline: This model is written in American English; the German its site and chat offer is translated from it, outside the model.

entities.name: Answering
entities.tagline: How a visitor's question about the company is answered from the model, by an agent, with nothing added and nobody reading the answer before it goes out.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never lets a claim stand that no tool returned in that conversation.
- Never keeps a conversation or an answer; the tab holds the conversation and the meter counts only what was spent.
- Never keeps more of a question than the question itself and whether the model could answer it, never with an address and never past ninety days, as the privacy page says.
- Never spends past the ceiling the deployment wrote down, and refuses before asking the model.
- Never answers from a model commit other than the one the host pins.

entities.name: Answer
entities.tagline: Give the visitor what the model says, in their words, and not a claim more.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A message the fence has let through: under the length it allows, from a page the deployment names, inside the hour's, the day's and the month's share. The host's tools, at its pinned commit.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Visitor asks, in their own words and language.
2. The Answerer asks the host's tools, up to four rounds: a kind of thing by its type, a named thing by search and then the entity itself.
3. The Answerer writes the answer from what the tools said, naming the entity each claim rests on, and where they said nothing, that the model does not say.
4. The page links each entity the answer was read from, to the model page and to the file at the commit.
5. Where the deployment checks its answers, each claim is read back against the tool answers that carried the entities it names, and the page marks one the evidence does not carry.
6. Nobody reads the answer before the Visitor does. The Owner's gate was passed once, before any question: the rules the seat runs under, the commit the host pins, the fence, and the switch that stops the chat without a deploy.

rows: In the visitor's tab, in their language, every claim traceable to a tool's answer in that conversation; gone when the tab closes
In the visitor's tab, in their language, every claim traceable to a tool's answer in that conversation; gone when the tab closes

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never sends a message before the visitor presses send, and never reads one they did not.
- Never answers a question that is not about the model with more than a sentence saying what the chat is for.
- Never continues past the ceiling: a spent share is a refusal, made before the model is asked.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
Answer is the only phase. An answer has left it when:

- Every claim in it names the entity a tool returned it from.
- Where the tools did not say, it says the model does not say.
- It was written inside the fence: the rounds, the output length and the share.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: The rules or the model are corrected through Delivery, and the chat opens again; no answer is corrected after the fact, because none is kept.

entities.name: Reply
entities.tagline: One answer in a visitor's tab, in their language, read from the model at the host's commit and kept nowhere.

entities.name: Contribution
entities.tagline: How a change offered from outside as a pull request is reviewed and taken, under the same rules a change from inside is held to.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never merges anything with a red check or no check.
- Never treats a review finding as a verdict; it is an input to whoever merges, and silence is a valid answer to one.
- Never claims an interest in what a contributor describes in the vocabulary.

entities.name: Consider
entities.tagline: Establish what the change is for, before anyone spends time on how it is written.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A pull request against the default branch, from anyone, with a description saying what is now true that was not before.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Owner reads the description before the diff, because a change whose purpose is unclear cannot be reviewed for whether it achieves it.
2. The Owner establishes whether the change is wanted at all, and says so early; a review of something that will not be taken spends a contributor's evening for nothing.
3. The Owner names which rules it will be held to, where the contributor may not know them — the register a text is written in, the form the Markdown takes, the schema an entity answers to.
4. The Owner checks that the status check reports, and that it is the contributor's own commit under their own address.

rows: A statement that the change is wanted, or that it is not and why, written in the pull request
A statement that the change is wanted, or that it is not and why, written in the pull request

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never reviews the writing of a change it has not decided is wanted.
- Never leaves a contributor to discover a rule from a failing check that could have been named.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Consider, all of these hold:

- The pull request says what is now true that was not before.
- The Owner or the Partner has said the change is wanted.
- The status check has reported.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: The Owner says which of the criteria failed, with what would make a later pull request succeed.

entities.name: Integrate
entities.tagline: Take the change into the default branch, and carry it to whoever vendors what it touched.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A change whose findings the Owner has ruled on, with one green check.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. On the Owner's word the change is merged with a merge commit, never a squash, so the address the contributor committed under reaches the default branch unchanged.
2. Where the change touches what another repository vendors or builds from, a release is tagged on the Owner's word, with notes the Owner has read: a minor where a consumer re-syncs or re-pins, a major where it is asked to do more than either, and the notes say which.
3. The Owner moves every pin that names the release, each in a commit that says why, and every surface built from one of them is rebuilt at the commit it now names.
4. The Owner deletes the branch, as their own step.

rows: The change on the default branch, carrying the author it was given
Where something vendored moved: a tag and notes saying what a consumer must do
The change on the default branch, carrying the author it was given
Where something vendored moved: a tag and notes saying what a consumer must do

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text: - Never leaves a pin behind a release without recording that it is deliberately behind.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Integrate, all of these hold:

- The default branch carries the change under the address its author committed with.
- Where something vendored moved, a release exists and its notes say what a consumer must do.
- Every pin that names the release has moved with it, or is recorded as deliberately behind.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: The Owner reverts rather than leave the default branch in a state nobody chose.

entities.name: Propose
entities.tagline: Offer the change, under the address the Contributor means to be known by.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: The repository, its conventions and its schemas, all of which are published and need nobody's permission to read.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Contributor branches from the default branch and makes the change there.
2. The Contributor writes what is now true that was not before, as the pull request's description.
3. The Contributor commits under their own address, which is theirs to choose and nobody else's to set.
4. The Contributor opens the pull request and lets the check run.

rows: A change against the default branch, saying what is now true that was not, under its author's own address
A change against the default branch, saying what is now true that was not, under its author's own address

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never merges, tags or releases.
- Never has to have read every convention first; where one was missed, naming it is the company's work.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Propose, all of these hold:

- A pull request exists against the default branch.
- It says what is now true that was not before.
- Its commits carry the address their author means to be known by.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: Nothing here obliges anyone to finish what they started.

entities.name: Review
entities.tagline: Find what is wrong with the change, and hand it to whoever merges as findings rather than as a verdict.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A change the Owner has said is wanted, with its check reporting.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Reviewer reads the change against what the pull request says it does, and reports where the two disagree.
2. The Reviewer writes one finding per comment, each with a severity and the line it sits on.
3. The Reviewer judges what no check reads: whether an entity answers its schema's writing rules, and whether a text is in the register its place calls for.
4. The Reviewer says what it could not verify, rather than leaving a reader to assume it was checked.

rows: One per comment, each with a severity and the line it sits on, addressed to whoever merges
One per comment, each with a severity and the line it sits on, addressed to whoever merges

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never merges, and never approves in a way that reads as merging.
- Never states a finding as a decision the contributor must take.
- Never asks for a change of taste as though it were a rule.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Review, all of these hold:

- Every finding carries a severity and the line it sits on.
- The Owner or the Partner has read the findings and said which are to be acted on.
- What the review could not verify is written down.

entities.name: Change
entities.tagline: A change to what this company publishes, offered from outside as a pull request, in code or in prose.

entities.name: Deciding
entities.tagline: How the Owner decides what comes next, from an overview of all open work checked at the moment of asking, because building fast is solved and deciding well is not.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text: - Never puts more than one decision to the Owner at a time.

entities.name: Carry
entities.tagline: Do what the Owner's word covers, tell whoever it touches, and report what happened.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: The Owner's word from Propose. Where an action the word covers is refused by the seat's permissions, the seat stops there and hands the Owner what is left.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Surveyor checks the state the action touches once more, right before acting on it.
2. The Surveyor carries out what the word covers; a commit it makes is made in the seat whose work it carries.
3. The Surveyor tells the sessions the change touches what changed.
4. The Surveyor reports to the Owner what was done, with the commits and pull requests it made, and any mistake it made on the way.

rows: What the Owner's word covered, done; finished when the state it changed has been read back
What was done and what went wrong, each linked to where it can be read
What the Owner's word covered, done; finished when the state it changed has been read back
What was done and what went wrong, each linked to where it can be read

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text: - Never leaves out of the report a mistake made on the way.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
- What the word covered is done and read back from where it is held.
- The sessions it touches were told.
- The Owner has the report.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: An action the seat's permissions refuse is handed to the Owner with the commands that would do it.

entities.name: Propose
entities.tagline: Put one decision to the Owner with a recommendation, and take the Owner's word on it.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: An overview that has passed Survey. Where the overview is older than the question now asked, it goes back to Survey first.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Surveyor names the one decision that comes next and what it changes.
2. The Surveyor recommends one answer and says why, and names the other answers it set aside.
3. The Owner decides: yes, no, wait, or an answer of their own.

rows: One decision with one recommended answer and the reason for it
The answer the Owner gave, in their words; finished when it says what may be done
One decision with one recommended answer and the reason for it
The answer the Owner gave, in their words; finished when it says what may be done

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never puts a second decision to the Owner before the first is answered.
- Never takes an earlier word of the Owner's as the answer to this decision.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text: - The Owner has answered the decision put to them.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: A wait is a decision too, and the process ends with nothing carried out.

entities.name: Survey
entities.tagline: Find out where the open work stands now, not where it stood when it was last looked at.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: The Owner's question, and read access to the repositories, pull requests, branches, worktrees and sessions it touches. Where the seat cannot read one of them, it starts anyway and names what it could not see.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Surveyor reads the state the question touches where it is held: the pull request on GitHub, the branch in its worktree, the session in its own words.
2. The Surveyor reads the memory for what was settled before, and checks each settled thing it relies on against its current state.
3. The Surveyor sets out the overview: what is open, in what state, who is working on it, each claim linked to where it was read.

rows: What is open, its state and who is working on it, each claim linked to where it was read; finished when nothing in it was taken from an earlier check
What is open, its state and who is working on it, each claim linked to where it was read; finished when nothing in it was taken from an earlier check

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text: - Never proposes; a choice it finds open is set out for Propose.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
- Every claim in the overview was checked in this conversation and links to where it was read.
- What the seat could not see is named.

entities.name: Decision
entities.tagline: One choice the Owner made, with the overview it was made on and what was done because of it.

entities.name: Delivery
entities.tagline: How anything we publish is shaped, specified, planned, made and merged, in code and in prose.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text: - Never begins a phase whose predecessor's gate neither the Owner nor the Partner has approved.

entities.name: Implement
entities.tagline: Make the thing, and let nothing go forward unread.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: An approved plan, a branch in a worktree of its own, and for each task the brief that is the whole of its requirements.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
### Code

1. The Controller dispatches one brief.
2. The Implementer works it, test first where the brief says so, and reports what was built, what was run and what it doubts.
3. The Reviewer reads the diff against the brief and returns findings, each with a file, a line and a severity, strengths named first.
4. Where the task touched a model, the Reviewer also reads every entity it touched against its schema's writing rules, which the mechanical checks do not reach.
5. The Controller decides: fix, accept or park for the Owner.
6. The task is committed before the next one is dispatched.
7. A finding against a task already committed comes back as its own brief; the commit stands and the fix is a new one.

### Prose

1. The Writer drafts the English from the brief, on the branch, and reports which claims it could not trace to the brief or to prose we have already published.
2. An entry of the model goes to the Owner on its own: what it says, the case against it, a proposal, and the Owner decides.
3. The Owner reviews on the branch, in the diff and, where a surface carries the text, on the rendered page.
4. The Translator makes the Swiss Standard German from the reviewed English only, one element at a time, with the glossary open, and hands back a back-translation beside each element.
5. An English edit re-runs the Translator on that element alone.

rows: One per task, on the branch, with every finding resolved or parked
The draft the Owner has read on the branch and, where a surface carries it, on the page
For a surface that carries it: made from the reviewed English, with its back-translation
One per task, on the branch, with every finding resolved or parked
The draft the Owner has read on the branch and, where a surface carries it, on the page
For a surface that carries it: made from the reviewed English, with its back-translation

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never changes a test's expectation to make it pass.
- Never dispatches the next task while the last one's findings are open.
- Never commits a change to a model that no validation pass has read.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Implement, all of these hold:

- Every task's findings are resolved, or parked for the Owner and named in the pull request.
- The repository's checks pass on the branch.
- Where a model changed, both halves of the validation pass have run over it: the mechanical checks, and an agent reading each entity against its schema's writing rules.
- The branch does what the specification said, and nothing else.

entities.name: Integrate
entities.tagline: Put the change where it binds, release what other repositories take from it, and move everything that names it.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A branch that left Implement with its checks green, and the specification it was made from.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Reviewer reviews the whole branch against the specification, not task by task.
2. The Controller opens the pull request and stops.
3. The Owner reads the diff and, where a surface carries the change, the rendered page, and gives the word; the merge follows, with a merge commit.
4. Where the change touches what another repository vendors or builds from, a release is tagged on the Owner's word, with notes the Owner has read: a minor where a consumer re-syncs or re-pins, a major where it is asked to do more than either, and the notes say which.
5. The Owner moves every pin that names the release, each in a commit that says why, and every surface built from one of them is rebuilt at the commit it now names.
6. The Owner deletes the branch and its worktree, as their own step.

rows: On the default branch, with its checks green
Where one is due: the tag, notes saying whether a consumer re-syncs, re-pins or does more, and every pin that names it moved
Where a surface is built from what changed: rebuilt at the commit it names, so the page and the model agree
On the default branch, with its checks green
Where one is due: the tag, notes saying whether a consumer re-syncs, re-pins or does more, and every pin that names it moved
Where a surface is built from what changed: rebuilt at the commit it names, so the page and the model agree

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text: - Never leaves a consumer pinned to a release that no longer exists.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
Integrate is the last phase. The work is done when all of these hold:

- The checks pass on the pull request.
- It is merged on the Owner's word.
- Where a release was due it is tagged, and its notes say whether a consumer re-syncs, re-pins or does more.
- Every pin that names the release has moved with it, or is recorded as deliberately behind, and every surface built from one of them has been rebuilt.

entities.name: Plan
entities.tagline: Cut the approved specification into pieces that can be worked one at a time.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A specification or brief the Owner has approved, and the repository the work lands in with the rules that bind it.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
### Code

1. The Planner maps the files the change creates and modifies, and what each is responsible for.
2. The Planner cuts the work into task briefs, each the whole of its own requirements.
3. The Planner names the interfaces each brief produces and consumes, so no brief depends on a conversation its holder did not have.
4. The Planner orders them so each can be worked, tested and committed on its own.
5. Where the change reaches another repository, the pin that moves is a brief of its own, because it lands in a repository of its own and after the release.

### Prose

1. The Planner names the entries that change, and in what order.
2. The Planner cuts them one to a brief, because an entry is put to the Owner on its own.
3. The Planner names which of them a surface carries in German, and so which the Translator is run on.

rows: An ordered set, each whole on its own, each with a way to tell it is done
An ordered set, each whole on its own, each with a way to tell it is done

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never re-opens a decision the specification took.
- Never writes a brief whose holder would have to guess at an interface.
- Never writes the change.
- Never plans a task whose completion cannot be checked.
- Never puts two entries of the model in one brief.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Plan, all of these hold:

- The Owner or the Partner has read the plan and approved it.
- Every brief states how its holder can tell the task is done.
- The order is one the briefs can actually be worked in.

entities.name: Shape
entities.tagline: Decide what kind of change this is, how far it reaches, and how much of it gets written down.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A request in whatever words it arrived in, and the part of the model, the vocabulary or the repository it will have to agree with, read rather than remembered.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Owner states the request as one sentence.
2. The Owner classifies it: a question whose output is an answer, a bounded change to something already here to read or a change to how things fit together.
3. The Owner names the track it runs on.
4. The Owner names how far it reaches: what another repository vendors or builds from, and what surface is rebuilt from a commit of it.
5. The Owner says which phases write a document and which are satisfied in conversation.
6. The Owner names what is explicitly not being changed.

rows: Which of the three kinds of change this is, and why
Which track the work runs on, named as the process spells it
What the change makes stale: what vendors it, what builds from it, and what is rebuilt when it lands
Which phases produce a file and which are answered in conversation
Which of the three kinds of change this is, and why
Which track the work runs on, named as the process spells it
What the change makes stale: what vendors it, what builds from it, and what is rebuilt when it lands
Which phases produce a file and which are answered in conversation

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never classifies by how familiar the work feels rather than by what exists to read.
- Never lets a classification skip a gate; only the document scales, never the approval.
- Never begins the work it is classifying.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Shape, all of these hold:

- The request is stated as one sentence.
- The track is named.
- What the change makes stale is named, or named as nothing.
- The classification is stated, and the phases that will write a document are named.

entities.name: Spec
entities.tagline: Write what the change must do, completely enough that nobody downstream has to guess.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A classified request, the model and the vocabulary the change must not contradict, and whatever it will touch, read rather than remembered.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
### Code

1. The Specifier reads the model, the vocabulary and the code the change lands in, before proposing anything.
2. The Specifier names the approaches worth considering, with their trade-offs, and recommends one.
3. The Specifier writes the specification: the gap, the decisions and their reasons, what was rejected and why, and what is explicitly not being done.
4. Where the change adds vocabulary, the specification names the company nobody could describe without it and the instance that will be written against it.
5. Where the change reaches what another repository vendors or builds from, the specification says what the release will ask of a consumer: a re-sync, a re-pin or more than either.
6. The Specifier parks every question that is the Owner's, rather than answering it conveniently.

### Prose

1. The Specifier names the audience, the one point, the facts the text may claim and where each is shown.
2. For an entry of the model, each fact is traced to prose we have already published, because nothing here is invented.
3. The Specifier names the file and the place it lands, and the register the place calls for.
4. The Specifier names the claims it may not make.

rows: The whole of the requirements for a change to code, with what is not being done named
For prose: the audience, the one point, the facts it may claim and where each is shown
The whole of the requirements for a change to code, with what is not being done named
For prose: the audience, the one point, the facts it may claim and where each is shown

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never writes the change it specifies.
- Never decides a question that is the Owner's; it names the options and parks it.
- Never leaves a question unasked because an assumption would be convenient.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Spec, all of these hold:

- The Owner or the Partner has read the specification or the brief and approved it.
- What is explicitly not being done is written down.
- Where the change reaches another repository, what its release asks of a consumer is written down.
- Every parked question has the word of the Owner or the Partner on it.

entities.name: Code
entities.tagline: A merged change to one of the repositories we publish, with its checks green, and where it changes what another repository vendors, the release that carries it.

entities.name: Prose
entities.tagline: An entry of the model, a schema, a README or a page of a site, in English the Owner has reviewed, and in Swiss Standard German where the surface carries it.

entities.name: Feature request
entities.tagline: How somebody outside asks for vocabulary or tooling that is not there, as a GitHub issue, and gets an answer they can act on.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never answers a request before knowing which page the asker could not write.
- Never promises a release date or a place on the roadmap; naming the release a chosen gap is aimed at is not a promise.
- Never closes a request without the reason written where it was asked.
- Never adds vocabulary because it was asked for; a request is evidence of a gap and never the decision to fill it.

entities.name: Answer
entities.tagline: Give the asker something they can act on, whether or not anything will be built.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A classified gap with its reason.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Owner writes the answer in the issue: what was decided, why, and what the asker can do now.
2. Where the gap is real and will be filled, the Owner says which release it is aimed at only if one has been chosen, and otherwise says that it has not been.
3. Where the gap is real and will not be filled, the Owner says what would change that.
4. Where there is no gap, the Owner names the type that already carries the fact and how it is written.
5. The Owner closes the issue.

rows: The decision, its reason and what the asker can do now, written where the request was made
The decision, its reason and what the asker can do now, written where the request was made

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never closes with a label and no sentence.
- Never leaves the asker without something to do, even where the answer is no.
- Never promises a date that has not been chosen.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Answer, all of these hold:

- The answer says what was decided and why, in the issue.
- The asker has something to do next, or is told plainly that there is nothing.
- No date appears that has not actually been chosen.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: An answer nobody can act on is not an answer, and closing the issue does not make it one.

entities.name: Raise
entities.tagline: Say where it can be answered that the vocabulary would not carry something.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: Whatever the Requestor was trying to describe and could not, in whatever words they have for it.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Requestor opens an issue on the repository the request concerns.
2. The Requestor says what they were trying to describe and where they stopped, in their own words.
3. The Requestor adds whatever makes that concrete — the page they were writing, the fact that had nowhere to go — and nothing they were not asked for.

rows: A GitHub issue on the repository it concerns, saying what could not be described
A GitHub issue on the repository it concerns, saying what could not be described

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never has to be written in the vocabulary's terms; putting it in them is the company's work.
- Never waits for a template, a label or a form; there is none, by design.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Raise, all of these hold:

- An issue exists, in the open, on the repository the request concerns.
- It says what the Requestor was trying to describe and could not.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: The Owner helps state it rather than closing it; a request nobody could phrase is still a finding about the vocabulary.

entities.name: Triage
entities.tagline: Decide what kind of thing the gap is, and whether it is ours to fill.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A restated request naming what could not be written.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Owner decides which of four the gap is: vocabulary every kind of company needs, vocabulary only some kinds need, tooling, or no gap at all.
2. The Owner checks whether an existing type already carries the fact under another name, because a request for a second name for one thing is a finding about the first.
3. The Owner weighs it against the strategy: vocabulary enters core once a company has actually had to be described with it, so one request is evidence and is not yet that.
4. The Owner writes the classification and its reason in the issue.

rows: Which of the four the gap is, with the reason, written in the issue
Which of the four the gap is, with the reason, written in the issue

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never classifies a gap as core vocabulary on the strength of one request.
- Never leaves the reason out because the classification seems obvious.
- Never opens a specification; what happens next is Delivery's, and it starts from its own Shape.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Triage, all of these hold:

- The gap is classified as core vocabulary, pack vocabulary, tooling or no gap.
- The reason is written where the request was made.
- Where it is core vocabulary, the instance that had to be described with it is named.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: The Owner says what would settle it, rather than classifying it to be finished with it.

entities.name: Understand
entities.tagline: Turn what somebody asked for into the page they could not write.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A GitHub issue on the repository the request is about, from anyone, in whatever words they brought.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Owner reads the request as it was written, before restating it.
2. The Owner establishes what the asker was trying to describe and could not — the entity, the field or the rule that was missing when they stopped.
3. The Owner asks for that where it is absent, and asks for nothing else; a request is not a form to be completed.
4. The Owner restates the request as the gap it is, in the issue, and lets the asker correct the restatement.

rows: The request written as the page that could not be written, agreed with whoever raised it
The request written as the page that could not be written, agreed with whoever raised it

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never rewrites the asker's words as the record; the restatement sits beside them.
- Never decides whether the gap is real.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
To leave Understand, all of these hold:

- The request names the entity, the field or the rule that was missing.
- Whoever raised it has seen the restatement and not disputed it.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: The Owner says so in the issue; not understood is an answer, and is not a refusal.

entities.name: Decision
entities.tagline: An answer written where the request was made, in the words the request used, saying what was decided and why.

entities.name: Narrating
entities.tagline: How a talk's reviewed speaker notes become the clips a visitor hears, in English and in German, with every clip heard by the Owner before it ships.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never speaks a note that has not been reviewed in its language.
- Never speaks a clip again whose text, voice, model and settings are unchanged.
- Never ships a clip the Owner has not listened to.

entities.name: Narrate
entities.tagline: Turn each changed note into a clip in its language, and let none of them out unheard.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A deck whose English notes are reviewed and whose German notes were made from them and reviewed, both on a branch. The cues in a note are the author's directions for where to pause.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.text:
1. The Narrator reads each slide's note from the deck, in each language; a cue becomes a paragraph break or a direction to the voice.
2. The Narrator skips a slide whose stamp still matches its note, voice, model and settings, so an edited note costs one clip and not a deck.
3. The Narrator speaks each remaining note in its language's voice and treats a click at the end of a clip.
4. The Owner listens to every new clip in the deck, in both languages.

rows: One per changed slide and language, beside the deck, with the stamp that says what it was spoken from; finished when the Owner has heard it
One per changed slide and language, beside the deck, with the stamp that says what it was spoken from; finished when the Owner has heard it

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never lets one clip that fails stop the rest of the deck.
- Never regenerates a whole deck to change one clip.

sections.heading: Gate
sections.text:
- The Owner has listened to every new clip.
- Every clip's stamp matches the note on its slide.

sections.heading: If not met
sections.text: A note that changes goes back through Delivery.

entities.name: Clip
entities.tagline: One slide's note, spoken in one language, beside the deck it belongs to and stamped with what it was spoken from.

entities.name: Software
entities.tagline: What CompanyGraph ships to be installed and run: the metamodel package with its checks, server, plugin and tooling.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text: A product of this kind is opened by the people who run a company and the agents beside them, by vendoring it into their own repository and running what it ships. CompanyGraph Core is this kind. There is no other kind yet; consulting, were it ever a product, would be a second.

entities.name: CompanyGraph Core
entities.tagline: The vocabulary for describing a company as a graph of Markdown files, with the checks, the agent access and the editing support that read it, used by the people who run a company and the agents working beside them.

entities.name: AI Agent
entities.tagline: Surveys the open work for the Owner, and specifies, plans, runs, implements, reviews, drafts and translates what this company publishes, answers whoever asks about it, under a rulebook for each, and decides nothing.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text:
It holds the Surveyor's seat in Deciding, every seat in Delivery but the Owner's, and none in the two processes that begin outside the company: a request is raised by a person and a change is offered by one. Whichever model runs it, the rulebooks are the same, every question it parks ends with the Owner's word, and nothing it produces reaches the default branch without the Owner merging it.

This profile is here so the model can say what holds a seat, as Robert Blust's says who holds the Owner's; a seat no profile names is held by whichever person brings the work to it.

entities.name: Fit
entities.tagline: Questions a company asks before it decides CompanyGraph is for it: what problem it solves, how it differs from what the company already has, and whether it fits the company's own shape.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
A question about the problem and the match: why a model rather than a wiki, what a company would use it for, what a company's model looks like, whether the vocabulary fits and whether a pack holds what a company of its kind needs, whether a model can be kept in several languages, whether it helps with the EU AI Act, where targets and actual numbers go, how content stays current and who keeps it true, and whether it works with the agent and the graph database a company already runs.

How to begin is Getting started. What it costs, who is behind it and how it proves itself is Terms.

A question about the first steps and what connects once the model exists: starting an instance, what a page is written in, writing a profile, letting an agent read it and whether one may change it, and whether the data leaves the company's hands when it runs.

Whether it fits at all is Fit. Price, license and the people behind it are Terms.
